entry.title: Resolving cell states in spatial transcriptomics with SCATTER
entry.summary: A capture spot can contain transcripts from multiple cell types. Differences between spots may reflect changes in cell-type proportions, expression within a cell type, or both, making local cell-type expression difficult to infer from mixed counts. We developed SCATTER to estimate cell-type proportions and relative expression profiles for each cell type at each spot from spatial transcriptomic counts, coordinates, and annotated single-cell reference data. SCATTER weights reference cell profiles using local spatial context, then jointly fits the resulting profiles and cell-type proportions to reconstruct spot counts. Cell2location estimates regularize the proportions. After fitting, SCATTER uses learned gene-specific calibration factors and fitted proportions to allocate observed counts among cell types. In five pseudo-spot benchmarks constructed from imaging data, SCATTER achieved higher cross-spot correlations with measured expression for 82.8-99.8% of evaluated gene-cell type pairs in pairwise comparisons with DestVI, PANDA, and STged. In breast cancer Xenium data, it recovered gene expression associated with the tumor neighborhood and regulon scores. In breast cancer Visium data, inferred stromal and macrophage expression showed distinct associations with neighborhood malignant cell proportions. In multiple sclerosis brain tissue, SCATTER recovered lesion-associated glial expression programs. In colorectal cancer Visium HD data, it mapped cell-type-specific programs at the invasive front and ranked candidate ligand-receptor pairs. SCATTER enables analysis of spatial expression variation within cell types from mixed tissue measurements.
entry.arxiv:comment: 40 pages, 6 figures, 1 table; supplementary information included

entry.title: Stochastic Failure Dynamics in a Model Peptidoglycan Mesh under Hydrolysis and Mechanical Loading
entry.summary: We develop a minimal stochastic-mechanical model for failure dynamics of the Gram-negative peptidoglycan (PG) cell wall under blocked growth and continued hydrolysis. The cell wall is modelled as a collection of load-bearing cross-sections, with random number of cross-links in each such cross-section, around a fixed degree of cross-linking. To understand failure dynamics of the cell wall under antibacterial agents which prevent insertion of fresh PG material, peptide bonds are progressively excised by hydrolases, while insertion/formation of new bonds is blocked. We compare and contrast rupture dynamics in no-load and load-activated regimes, using extreme value theory and stochastic simulations, deriving limiting laws for system failure in both the long-cell and large crosslinking limits. For a cross-section with many bonds, the mean failure time grows only log- arithmically with bond number, giving diminishing returns from additional cross-linking. In the no-load case, the centered failure time converges to a Gumbel law, though crucially, load changes the centered distribution and accelerates the final stages of collapse. In long cells, failure follows a weakest-link Weibull-type scaling controlled by the least cross-linked regions, with mechanical load reducing the failure-time scale without changing the weakest-link exponent. The fraction of bonds removed before failure tends to zero, showing that collapse can remain highly localized even while the global cross-linking degree stays high. Slowing down growth and other cellular functions is a typical antibiotic escape mechanism for bacteria and in this context, we show that, hydrolase down-regulation uniformly rescales the failure-time distribution and delays collapse, but does not remove the load-induced preference for rupture in weakened regions.

entry.title: Did the Model Forecast It, or Already Know It? Evaluating Large Language Models for Novel Drug-Target Prioritisation with a Temporal Knowledge-Graph Oracle
entry.summary: AI systems increasingly help decide which drug targets enter costly clinical trials. We recast each target-disease hypothesis as a dated event, the pair's first clinical trial. This lets us test whether a language model can forecast such events after its training cutoff, rather than recall events before it. We rebuild a dated biomedical knowledge graph as it stood at the end of each year from 2020 up to its newest version. We then ask six open language models, with and without this graph, which targets will enter a first trial for a disease the next year. Without retrieval, the models rank about as well as trial history, a count of each target's past trials in the same therapeutic area, also after their training cutoffs. Evidence dated before the decision adds at most a small gain, before or after the models' training cutoffs. The newest graph raises five of six models clearly above that baseline, but its paths usually include the answer: the pair's own trial, dated after the decision. Evaluations of target prioritisation should date both features and labels, with evidence from before the decision and outcomes after it.
entry.arxiv:comment: 14 pages, 7 figures, 5 tables. Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on AI for Drug Discovery: Bridging the Translation Gap (AI4DD). Code and data: https://github.com/jackysiupuichung/forecast-or-know

entry.title: Cell-Type-Specific Expression Is Hard to Predict from Bulk, but It Is Still Useful
entry.summary: Single-cell-informed deconvolution provides cell-type-resolved features for clinical bulk RNA cohorts. Most existing methods predict the proportions $π_k$ of the $K$ constituent cell types (CTs). Fewer predict cell-type-specific expression (CTSE) $μ_{kg}$ of gene $g$ in CT $k$, which can capture cell states that proportions miss, but recent benchmarks find it much harder. We explain this gap with closed-form accuracy bounds. For CTSE, we derive an $R^2$ ceiling for per-gene linear estimators. For proportions, the best linear estimator, which pools evidence across genes, has a closed-form $R^2$, and a computable lower bound on it predicts which CTs are learnable. We study targeted deconvolution of 106 biologically curated (CT, gene) pairs, found post hoc to have higher learnability scores. On overall survival in non-small cell lung cancer, estimation difficulty does not predict prognostic value across these targets. Yet a sparse survival model on deconvolved features, mostly CTSE, predicts survival as well as a sparse model on the bulk genes themselves, while attributing its signal to specific cell types. Some deconvolved CTSE features reveal prognostic signal not seen in the corresponding bulk gene.
entry.arxiv:comment: Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on AI for Drug Discovery (AI4DD). 5 pages main text, 28 pages total

entry.title: Milk-removal feedback shapes lactation sustainability and daily output in a model of human lactation
entry.summary: Milk production during lactation is dynamically regulated by milk removal, yet quantitative models linking feeding or pumping schedules to subsequent production remain scarce. We develop a minimal model describing milk accumulation and production between removal sessions, and the stimulation of subsequent production through milk removal. We compare different assumptions about how stimulation depends on the amount of milk removed or the duration of removal, and consider two removal protocols: prescribing either the removed amount or the removal duration. When stimulation depends on the removed amount, declining production can reduce subsequent stimulation and reinforce the decline. This leads to a critical wait interval beyond which no repeated constant schedule can sustain lactation. If stimulation is inefficient for small removal amounts but more efficient at intermediate amounts, the model can exhibit bistability: depending on the initial conditions, milk production either persists or ceases. In contrast, duration-dependent stimulation does not permit a zero-production state under continued removal, but can generate non-constant long-term dynamics under certain conditions. We further show that maximizing milk removal per session need not maximize daily output, because increased removal competes with session frequency. The framework provides a basis for testing alternative feedback hypotheses against longitudinal data and for optimizing feeding and pumping schedules.
entry.arxiv:comment: 65 pages (44 main + 21 appendix), 13 figures, 1 Supplementary html file

entry.title: Wasserstein-Fisher-Rao Reconstruction of Discrete space Population Dynamics
entry.summary: Reconstructing the continuous time dynamics of cell state evolution from sparse snapshot observations can be formulated as an unbalanced optimal transport problem. To study such dynamics at a coarse grained cell type level, unbalanced optimal transport must be extended to discrete state spaces. Inspired by discrete flow matching, we extended the dynamic Wasserstein-Fisher-Rao (WFR) problem to discrete spaces, and derived a closed form for its solution. For particularly large state spaces or more general models, we proposed an unbalanced discrete flow matching as a numerical approximation method, which provides a Markovian reconstruction of the optimal WFR flow. Our discrete WFR framework also stays stable across different coarse grain resolution. Finally, numerical experiments demonstrated the effectiveness of the proposed approach, and applications to real biological data supported the plausibility of the reconstructed dynamics.

entry.title: Exclusion and internal structure in the association/dissociation kinetics of DNA-binding proteins in the fast diffusion limit
entry.summary: In many canonical biophysical and biochemical contexts, complex diffusing DNA-binding proteins undergoing nonspecific adsorption and desorption can exist in different conformational states. Equilibrium binding theories and kinetic models of competing ligands provide a basis for describing these systems. Coupling the internal conformational kinetics of bound proteins to exclusion and diffusion requires tracking both protein positions and binding states. Closed-form, tractable mathematical models that accurately describe the stochastic dynamics of structured proteins that bind to and diffuse along DNA are lacking. Here, we develop a new coarse-grained stochastic model of nonspecific DNA-protein binding in the fast diffusion regime, from which we derive an effective Markov model and its corresponding mean-field approximation that incorporates protein footprint size and conformational switching. We fit our new model quantitatively to previously measured dynamics of Replication Protein A (RPA) binding to ssDNA. Finally, by including multisegment binding states, our analysis captures facilitated exchange, revealing how multisegment architecture balances high affinity with rapid remodeling. Our theoretical model applies broadly to many other DNA-binding protein systems, including nucleosomes, ssDNA-binding proteins, and other multisegment complexes, providing accurate predictions and new strategies for evaluating experimental data.

entry.title: Systematic study of the performance of small robots on controlled laboratory substrates
entry.summary: The design of robots able to locomote effectively over a diversity of terrain requires detailed ground interaction models; unfortunately such models are lacking due to the complicated response of real world substrates which can yield and flow in response to loading. To advance our understanding of the relevant modeling and design issues, we conduct a comparative study of the performance of DASH and RoACH, two small, biologically inspired, six legged, lightweight (10 cm, 20 g) robots fabricated using the smart composite microstructure (SCM) process. We systematically examine performance of both robots on rigid and flowing substrates. Varying both ground properties and limb stride frequency, we investigate average speed, mean mechanical power and cost of transport, and stability. We find that robot performance and stability is sensitive to the physics of ground interaction: on hard ground kinetic energy must be managed to prevent yaw, pitch, and roll instability to maintain high performance, while on sand the fluidizing interaction leads to increased cost of transport and lower running speeds. We also observe that the characteristic limb morphology and kinematics of each robot result in distinct differences in their abilities to traverse different terrains. Our systematic studies are the first step toward developing models of interaction of limbs with complex terrain as well as developing improved limb morphologies and control strategies.

entry.title: Using waveform types, discrete Sobolev distances, and trend compatibility to cluster short time series of clinical data
entry.summary: Clinical tests, such as the oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT), perturb a physiological system at rest and record its excursion over a fixed protocol window as a short, undersampled time series. Such curves rarely allow parameter identification at the individual level, yet their trends carry physiological information that emerges at the population level as recurrent response patterns. Standard clustering methods aggregate differences globally and average out those trends, losing precisely the information about how the system regains control after the perturbation; identifying response patterns requires a method that preserves them. We present a nonparametric framework that factorizes each curve into unit waveforms, sorts them with a symbolic trend-compatibility filter, and compares compatible shapes using discrete Sobolev-type distances on finite differences up to order $k$. The number of clusters, i.e., distinct response types, equals the number of realizable trend patterns the cohort populates, validated by resampling. Applied to 1283 five-point OGTTs, the method identifies 7 glycemia and 8 insulinemia types. The count holds across a threefold range of resolution. In benchmarks against six classical clustering methods, ours alone never mixes opposite trends, with comparable reconstruction error and stability. Clinical normality, assessed after clustering, is graded, overlapping, and distributed unevenly across response types ($h=0.14$--$0.48$). Overall, our method distinguishes response types among curves too short for alignment-based methods yet too informative for reduction to summary values. It applies to any protocol recording a system's response to a standardized perturbation on a short grid.

entry.title: DDxBasis: Explaining Frozen Foundation Encoder-based Medical Classification by Exact Differential Diagnosis
entry.summary: In differential diagnosis (DDx), a clinician explains a diagnosis by the few findings that separate it from the alternatives. Medical image classifiers cannot yet explain themselves this way. Existing explanations are either faithful but spread over hundreds of concepts, or compact but leave part of each decision unexplained. We present DDxBasis, which explains a classifier on a frozen foundation encoder as a differential diagnosis in three steps. First, a concept bottleneck reads all patch tokens at every encoder layer using gated, second-order slot attention. A concept basis then regroups the concepts into two-pole axes, each a differential between groups of diagnoses. Finally, we read a differential diagnosis from each axis through the typical presentation of its poles, the pertinent findings of the case, and counterfactual edits of borderline cases. Across five medical datasets, DDxBasis is the most accurate frozen-encoder model and close to the best published domain-specific results. Because every concept adds its own evidence, its reproducible concept basis splits each decision exactly, at no cost in accuracy. Without ordered stage or concept labels, the axes recover cell lineages and rare subtypes, agree with dermatologists' structure annotations, and expose planted and real shortcuts.

entry.title: Cell and nuclear shapes predict confined motility
entry.summary: Cancer metastasis relies on an enhanced property of cells to migrate efficiently even through constrictions smaller than their nucleus. Both cell and nuclear morphology may influence this process. How these morphologies relate to the likelihood that a cell will transit through a constriction remains unclear. Here we combine microfluidic experiments with machine learning to predict whether MDA-MB-231 breast cancer cells are able to transit through narrow constrictions. Cells migrate within vertically confined boxes, and may migrate into neighboring boxes by transiting through constrictions, requiring a deformation of the nucleus. Defining a set of 12 geometrical features derived from cell and nuclear contours, we find that their average values are not statistically indicative of whether or not a cell will transit. To overcome this limitation, we use trajectories to train classifiers and evaluate their ability to predict future transit events. We find that the cell area and cell circularity carry most of the predictive information and less circular cells are more likely to transit. Without retraining, the models also predict transit through narrower constrictions and in more adhesive substrates. Morphological features of cells about 30 minutes before a transit event proved most informative about future transit events occurring or not. Together, our results show that cell shape, readable from simple contour descriptors, contains a transferable but condition-dependent signature of imminent transit.

entry.title: PHM-ensemble: Scalable and Stable Probabilistic Multiresolution Clustering via Ensemble Density Estimation
entry.summary: Clustering is a foundational tool for exploratory data analysis across the sciences. We argue that clustering methods should be evaluated along four dimensions: fidelity to the data's underlying structure, interpretability of the recovered groups, stability under data perturbations and algorithmic randomness, and scalability to modern scientific datasets. Yet existing methods rarely satisfy all four criteria. To address this gap, we introduce PHM-ensemble, a general probabilistic framework for multiresolution clustering that estimates the underlying data density by pooling mixture models from an ensemble of fits and subsequently constructs a clustering hierarchy through hierarchical merging of the mixture components. On simulated datasets and the MNIST benchmark, PHM-ensemble matches or outperforms widely used clustering algorithms in agreement with ground truth, produces more stable results across runs, and reveals complex underlying structures. Applied to 1.82 million peripheral blood cells from the Human Immune Health Atlas, PHM-ensemble achieves higher agreement with expert-curated major cell-type annotations than the Leiden clustering used in the original study (adjusted Rand index 0.965 versus 0.789), while requiring only half the computing time. Beyond identifying major immune lineages, it reveals biologically coherent relationships among cell types and resolves finer structure within individual lineages, uncovering subtypes and cellular states consistent with known biology.

entry.title: Lattice models of chiral random motion: A short review
entry.summary: Chirality, a systematic rotational bias, is ubiquitous in many random motion patterns, from bacteria cells, that swim in circles near surfaces and spinning colloids, to charged particles diffusing under the influence of magnetic fields. In two dimensions, chirality renders random transport \textit{odd}: the diffusion tensor acquires an antisymmetric part that leaves the mean-squared displacement invariant but modifies fluxes and boundary currents. Lattice models for random motion are a natural setting to study chirality, since they are exactly solvable, connect directly to heterogeneous media, cellular automata, and programmable robots, and in discrete time admit fully chiral limits with a localised bulk and edge transport. Lattice walks with a rotational bias have been introduced in different communities several times since 1960, yet without a common language or conceptual connection between them. Here we review these models from the perspective that on the lattice, chirality requires memory. Taking the recently introduced chiral random walk model as a template, we describe the walker with an internal degree of freedom. With a chiral biased updating rule, the full diffusion tensor of this chiral walker turns odd. Within this picture, we can unite persistent and chiral walks, run-and-tumble motion, and cyclic random motions in one framework. We discuss how the memory is followed into the environment; in Lorentz lattice gases, kinetic and rotor walks, and random odd environments; and into the path; in spiral self-avoiding walks.

entry.title: Longitudinal Characterization of Personalized Hydration Dynamics Using a Facial-Video Digital Hydration Biomarker
entry.summary: Background. Hydration is often assessed at a single time point despite continuous changes in body water. A facial-video biomarker has tracked hydration-state transitions, but its longitudinal behavior is unclear. Objective. To assess within-person hydration score changes, individual differences in fluid response, and implications for personal calibration. Methods. Five adults completed water and electrolyte days with an identical 2.0 L fluid schedule, using facial videos every 30 minutes over 12 hours (250 videos). On a separate morning, each completed a 500 mL electrolyte challenge with baseline and four follow-up videos over 2 hours (25 videos). Analyses assessed trajectories, post-drink changes, variability, time at or above score 50, and exploratory effects of starting score and beverage day. Results. The first scan was the day's lowest on 7 of 10 days. Across 50 intakes, the mean post-drink change was +4.0 points, exceeding a shuffled-time comparison (p less than 0.001). For 21 intakes starting below 50, no subsequent score fell; the mean rise was +11.3 points versus +5.7 expected under permutation (p less than 0.001). Intakes starting at 50 or above showed no rise beyond chance. After 500 mL electrolytes, mean change over 2 hours was positive for all five participants, with peak increases of 7.2 to 22.6 points at 30 to 90 minutes. Despite identical fluid schedules, time at or above 50 ranged from 16% to 100%. The electrolyte day showed a greater mean increase from morning baseline than the water day (+7.7 points), although day order was fixed. Conclusion. Facial-video hydration scores showed longitudinal changes associated with drinking and marked individual differences. These exploratory findings support further research on personal calibration and hydration protocols in larger controlled studies.

entry.title: Benchmarking Protein Structure Tokenizers as Generation Targets for Language Models
entry.summary: Discrete structure tokenizers are the standard way to give a language model access to protein three-dimensional structure, yet they are selected on how accurately they can be read, their reconstruction fidelity, while the property that governs generation is how well a model can write them. We measure this property, writability, directly: holding the base model, data, recipe and compute fixed, we swap only the tokenizer and train the same 9B model to emit structure tokens residue by residue, over eight tokenizers, four compute budgets and three evaluation sets (96 cells). At 2B tokens final writability runs from TM 0.662 down to 0.378 under identical conditions, with five of the eight arms clearing the TM 0.5 mark at which a fold is usually called correct and three falling short of it. Neither codebook size nor reconstruction ceiling explains where an arm lands; the best and worst both use 8192 codewords. What does explain the spread is local structure preservation of the code space. In DPLM-2 a one-bit codeword error costs 0.019 TM where a random codeword costs 0.347, and the trained model's own errors are correspondingly local, at 0.51 of the random Hamming expectation; FoldToken4 fails both tests at the same codebook size and is 0.13 TM less writable. Three controls discipline how such a benchmark may be read. A same-recipe rerun puts the noise floor at $σ=0.0067$ TM, which collapses an apparent six-way ranking into four tiers. A reference-free geometry panel turns out to be nearly orthogonal to TM (Pearson $-0.58$), with the worst arm by TM producing the most physically valid backbones. And two pre-registered interventions are null for a reason the mechanism measurements reveal: the quantity they target saturates at 1.5B tokens while TM is still rising. All 131 evaluation cells, including raw generated token streams, are released.

entry.title: Tempering and few-shot calibration of pathology foundation models improve digital biomarker reproducibility across slide scanners
entry.summary: Pathology foundation models underpin a growing number of histology-based cancer biomarkers, but sensitivity to slide scanner-specific image signatures degrades cross-center reliability and reproducibility. We developed a foundation model fine-tuning method that improved consistency in head-and-neck cancer human papillomavirus (HPV) prediction, colorectal cancer microsatellite instability (MSI) identification, prostate cancer grading and breast cancer phenotyping. This tempering method decreased cross-scanner prediction differences by 67.5% for HPV (95% CI 59.0-73.9%), 69.3% for MSI (95% CI 51.9-76.5%) and 63.4%-81.2% for breast signatures. Cross-scanner prostate grade agreement rose from 42.5% to 92.7%. Under full scanner-HPV confounding during training, AUROC fell from 0.80 to 0.68 with original model features but only from 0.86 to 0.84 with tempering. Unlike post hoc feature calibration, tempering used only public data yet matched or exceeded on-site calibration. These findings support tempering to reduce scanner dependence of pathology foundation models.

entry.title: A multimodal foundation model for tissue proteomics and morphology in cancer
entry.summary: Cancer diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment decisions increasingly rely on integrating tissue morphology with specific molecular readouts of the tumor and its microenvironment. H&E histopathology provides scalable morphology, whereas multiplex spatial proteomics quantifies dozens of proteins in situ with spatial context, but remains selectively deployed, often with different marker panels across cohorts. This creates a translational bottleneck: most patients lack high-depth molecular profiling, and existing models rarely integrate morphology and spatial molecular data in a single framework. We present VirTues-M2, a multimodal foundation model that jointly learns from H&E and spatial proteomics using a novel vision transformer-based architecture. By encoding marker identity during pretraining, VirTues-M2 is robust to missing modalities, imperfect modality pairing or registration, and variable marker panels, enabling unified inference for tissue phenotyping, panoptic cell segmentation, virtual staining, annotation-free biomarker discovery, and reinforcement learning-based adaptive marker panel selection to reduce assay burden. As a concrete demonstration of translational utility, in a newly collected cohort of 1,053 treatment-naive non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) patients with paired spatial proteomics and H&E, VirTues-M2 discovers high-risk and low-risk tissue signatures that stratify overall survival in both the discovery cohort and an independent validation cohort, outperforming current state-of-the-art stratification schemes; all enabled by VirTues-M2's ability to jointly analyze both modalities within a single model.

entry.title: How Far Can Linear Go? BiPert, a Unified Framework for Single-Cell Perturbation Modelling
entry.summary: Understanding how genetic perturbations affect cellular behaviour is essential for studying gene function and regulatory mechanisms. Large-scale CRISPR screens measure these effects across thousands of genes, but cover relatively few cellular contexts. Predicting perturbation responses in unseen cell types and identifying perturbed genes from their transcriptional effects therefore remain challenging. Here, we show that both tasks can be addressed through a common linear decomposition of transcriptional responses into shared and perturbation-specific components. Building on this principle, we introduce BiPert, a simple linear framework for both forward perturbation prediction and inverse identification. For forward prediction, BiPert outperforms existing methods that use no external biological knowledge when predicting gene expression changes in unseen cell lines. Its few-shot extension, BiPert-FS, adapts to new cell lines using as few as ten measured perturbations. For inverse identification, BiPert-ID identifies perturbed genes from single-cell expression profiles, outperforming deep-learning methods in unseen cell lines and donors. We further show that perturbations whose effects transfer more consistently across cellular contexts are also easier to identify, even after controlling for perturbation effect size. Together, these results establish a connection between perturbation transfer and identification, and demonstrate that simple linear models provide strong, interpretable baselines for both tasks.

entry.title: Comparison of 3D-DXA Measurements with QCT Software Solutions for Proximal Femur Bone Density Assessment
entry.summary: 3D-Shaper reconstructs proximal femur shape and density in 3D from a standard hip dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) scan. In men and women aged 35-91 years, we compared 3D-Shaper integral volumetric bone mineral density (vBMD), trabecular vBMD, and cortical surface BMD (sBMD) with quantitative computed tomography (QCT) processed with three methods: an in-house pipeline, Stradview and QCTPro CTXA, which were used to derive bone measurements equivalent to those of 3D-Shaper. Agreement, including among QCT methods, was assessed with linear regression and Bland-Altman analysis (bias and limits of agreement, LoA). 3D-Shaper agreed strongly with the in-house pipeline and Stradview for integral vBMD (R=0.95-0.96; bias 1.5 to 4.2 mg/cm$^3$; LoA $\pm$39.7 to 41.4 mg/cm$^3$), trabecular vBMD (R=0.92-0.94; bias -11.8 to -7.8 mg/cm$^3$; LoA $\pm$33.3 to 39.4 mg/cm$^3$) and cortical sBMD (R=0.94; bias 5.6 to 38.2 mg/cm$^2$; LoA $\pm$23.6 to 26.4 mg/cm$^2$). The in-house pipeline and Stradview agreed for integral vBMD (R=1.00; bias -2.7 mg/cm$^3$; LoA $\pm$3.7 mg/cm$^3$), trabecular vBMD (R=0.96-1.00; bias -0.2 to 3.9 mg/cm$^3$; LoA $\pm$6.9 to 27.5 mg/cm$^3$) and cortical sBMD (R=0.98; bias 32.7 mg/cm$^2$; LoA $\pm$14.6 mg/cm$^2$). Compared with 3D-Shaper, QCTPro CTXA integral vBMD was systematically lower (R=0.90; bias -28.4 mg/cm$^3$; LoA $\pm$61.5 mg/cm$^3$) and trabecular vBMD showed a proportional bias (R=0.89; bias -44.1 mg/cm$^3$; LoA $\pm$61.3 mg/cm$^3$). The same pattern was observed against the other QCT methods, for integral vBMD (R=0.93; bias -32.6 to -29.9 mg/cm$^3$; LoA $\pm$49.6 to 50.0 mg/cm$^3$) and trabecular vBMD (R=0.94-0.96; bias -36.3 to -32.5 mg/cm$^3$; LoA $\pm$51.2 to 54.9 mg/cm$^3$). These findings support the agreement of 3D-Shaper with independent QCT approaches and show that 3D-Shaper-QCT differences must be interpreted in light of the QCT method used.

entry.title: Pesticide mixtures may compromise ecosystem services provided by an egg parasitoid of soybean pest stink bugs: a comprehensive ecotoxicological risk assessment
entry.summary: Tank mixtures of crop protection products are widely used in agricultural systems, yet their integrated effects on biological control agents remain poorly understood. We evaluated the lethal, sublethal, and transgenerational effects of four synthetic insecticides, applied alone or in binary mixtures with three fungicides and two herbicides, on adults and pupae of Telenomus podisi (Hymenoptera: Scelionidae), an important egg parasitoid of pest stink bugs. In adult bioassays, LC50 values ranged from 28.26 mg a.i. L-1 for isocycloseram + lambda-cyhalothrin to 265.88 mg a.i. L-1 for acephate. Overall, mixtures increased adverse effects relative to the individual products, reducing survival, parasitism, and longevity. The lowest parasitism rates occurred with isocycloseram + lambda-cyhalothrin combined with chlorothalonil or glyphosate SL formulation. Transgenerational effects were also detected, including reduced F1 emergence and an increased proportion of males in some treatments. Following pupal exposure, several mixtures reduced F0 emergence, whereas ethiprole + fenpropimorph and acephate + bixafen + prothioconazole + trifloxystrobin also reduced parasitism and longevity of the emerged adults. Integration of lethal and sublethal responses using the reduction coefficient (Ex) revealed increased toxicity for several mixtures and shifts in IOBC risk classification; notably, all insecticide + glyphosate mixtures reached Ex = 100% after pupal exposure. These findings show that assessing pesticides individually may underestimate ecotoxicological risk to T. podisi and highlight the need to consider pesticide mixtures in integrated pest management programs.

entry.title: GABIF: An Adaptive Guided Graph Denoising Framework for Antibody Conditional Inverse Folding
entry.summary: Antibodies play a central role in the human immune system, and their design is critical for vaccine development, therapeutic intervention, and improving human longevity. However, the vast combinatorial search space of antibodies poses a fundamental challenge for de novo discovery. Recent advances in deep learning, particularly denoising diffusion models, have demonstrated strong potential in protein inverse folding. Nevertheless, existing approaches are largely constrained to learning from natural antibody repertoires, thereby generating sequences that closely resemble natural antibodies. Such similarity, however, does not necessarily translate into improved functional performance in downstream applications. In this work, we develop a novel generative protein design model that enables the generation and optimization of antibody sequences tailored to specific downstream tasks and target metrics. Besides training on given an antibody dataset, we guide the generative model by an antibody-antigen binding affinity predictor for conditional discrete diffusion. The model is pre-trained on a given antibody dataset. Meanwhile, an antibody-antigen binding affinity predictor is incorporated as a conditional signal in a discrete diffusion framework, where a regressor serves as the conditional probability to guide the learning of the amino acid probability distribution of sequences under the objective of affinity optimization. In silico experiments demonstrate that our antibody design model achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art approaches, while the proposed regressor effectively improves binding affinity, as validated by an independent external predictor. Furthermore, our results highlight that the combination of finetuning and supervised guidance provides a powerful paradigm for adapting pretrained models to downstream tasks.

entry.title: Topological Pharmacokinetics: A Model-Free Framework for Quantifying the Shape of Concentration-Time Curves
entry.summary: Pharmacokinetic analysis compresses concentration-time curves into scalar summaries (non-compartmental analysis, NCA) or pre-specified compartmental models, approaches that are either model-free but shape-blind or shape-sensitive but structure-dependent. We introduce Topological Pharmacokinetics (TPK), a framework that reads curve shape directly from data without committing to any model. TPK delay-embeds each curve into a state-space trajectory and applies persistent homology to extract a nine-component topological invariant: multi-scale shape descriptors (peak hierarchy, secondary-peak isolation, loop structure) with established perturbation-stability properties. We evaluate the framework on four layers of increasing realism. Monophasic linear systems generate no spurious cyclic signals, whereas double-site absorption and enterohepatic recirculation produce distinct loop signatures; 12 nonlinear scenarios resolve as curvature-without-cycles; a weak endogenous rhythm survives superposition with a large exogenous drug signal (inter-peak interval recovered at exactly 24 h); and loop detection stays stable to 10 percent of Cmax additive noise and to sampling thinned to 7 points. As clinical proof of concept, we apply the same pipeline to 15 mycophenolic acid profiles digitized from a published kidney-transplant study. The secondary-persistence ratio associates with ex vivo gut-microbiome reactivation at Spearman rho = 0.815 (p = 0.0002, q = 0.002), whereas the tested exposure metrics show weak, nonsignificant associations (rho <= 0.38). Analyses are fully automated and reproducible; code and data are public. TPK is proposed as a complementary, model-free, shape-sensitive layer alongside NCA and model-based methods.

entry.title: Motivo: A Motif-Based Algorithm-Architecture Co-Design for Fast and Energy-Efficient Graph-Based Genome Analysis
entry.summary: Read mapping, a key step of genome sequence analysis, matches each fragment of a sequenced genome (a read) to its location in a reference genome. A genome graph is a graph-based reference genome that represents the genetic diversity of a population as alternative paths, and thus improves read mapping accuracy. However, the size and complexity of a genome graph make sequence-to-graph (S2G) mapping a major bottleneck. Prior software and hardware approaches for S2G mapping perform redundant costly operations (e.g., graph traversals and dynamic programming) that do not lead to valid mappings. Our key observation is that a genome graph consists of small subgraphs that share a limited set of recurring topologies, which we call motifs. We propose Motivo, a topology-aware algorithm-architecture co-design for S2G mapping. Motivo's algorithm uses motifs in two ways. First, it stores the precomputed motifs of each node in a compact index, which replaces a graph traversal with a single memory lookup. Second, it uses the topology of a motif and the properties of its nodes to identify the few most suitable mapping paths with arithmetic operations. The algorithm enables high-performance execution on CPUs and GPUs and high-performance, low-energy execution on Motivo-ASIC, an accelerator we co-design with it. Motivo-CPU provides 2.1-18.4x, 2.8-343x, and 1.4-10.1x speedups over GraphAligner, vg, and minigraph, and Motivo-GPU provides 1.5-1.6x speedups over vg-giraffe. Motivo-ASIC provides 7.4-11.7x (138-274x) speedups over state-of-the-art CPU-based tools for short (long) reads. Compared to SeGraM (short reads) and HARP (long reads), Motivo-ASIC achieves 5.3x and 4.0-4.3x higher throughput per Watt and 1.7x and 2.7-3.0x higher throughput per mm$^2$, respectively. Motivo maintains equal or higher mapping accuracy than other tools (96.8%-99.7%) for short and long reads on two types of genome graphs.

entry.title: Towards Edge Artificial Intelligence for Predicting Antimicrobial Resistance in Mycobacterium tuberculosis
entry.summary: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) in Mycobacterium tuberculosis (MTB) poses a major challenge to global tuberculosis control, as multidrug-resistant strains limit available treatment options. Rapid and accurate prediction of drug resistance from genomic data could support timely treatment decisions and public health interventions. However, many existing computational approaches for genomic AMR prediction rely on computationally intensive pipelines, limiting their suitability for deployment on resource-constrained edge devices. This limitation is particularly relevant in hospital settings in low- and middle-income countries, where computing infrastructure and access to high-performance computational resources may be limited. To address this challenge, we present a lightweight, novel machine learning (ML) approach suitable for running on edge devices that combines 4-mer frequency features derived from whole-genome sequences with a Random Forest classifier to predict antibiotic resistance in MTB. The proposed ML approach achieved an average area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.82 across 20 antibiotics on an independent test set.
entry.arxiv:comment: Accepted and Presented at the 11th IEEE Asia-Pacific Conference on Computer Science and Data Engineering (IEEE CSDE 2026), 1-3 November 2026, Cox's Bazar, Bangladesh

entry.title: SBTenv: A Literature-Validated Split-Belt Treadmill Simulation Environment
entry.summary: The split-belt treadmill is an important tool for studying human locomotor adaptation. Physics-based simulations complement such experiments by allowing hypotheses about the mechanisms of adaptation to be tested directly, and high-throughput simulation is increasingly needed as these models grow in complexity. However, no open-source split-belt treadmill environment exists in MuJoCo, a physics engine widely used for high-throughput simulation. Here, we present SBTenv, a split-belt treadmill environment built in MuJoCo and validated against published experimental data from a rimless wheel walking passively on a split-belt treadmill. By modeling compliant contacts at the spoke tips, SBTenv reproduces the experimental average steady velocity ($R^2=0.643$, RMSE $=0.0162$ m/s) without the empirical geometric correction required in prior simulations. We expect SBTenv, openly shared, to enable high-throughput simulation of musculoskeletal and robotic locomotion on a split-belt treadmill.
entry.arxiv:comment: 5 pages, 3 figures, 1 table. Code available at https://github.com/PhilipByrn3/sbtenv

entry.title: Critical slowing down in hive temperature does not provide actionable early warnings of honey bee colony collapse
entry.summary: Early warning signals (EWS) based on critical slowing down (CSD) have been proposed as model-independent indicators of approaching ecological regime shifts and may help anticipate honeybee colony collapse. However, whether theoretically expected signals can be reliably observed and provide useful prediction in real-world systems remains uncertain. Here, we combine structural analysis, mechanistic modeling and longitudinal observations to assess the dynamical plausibility, detectability and predictive accuracy of CSD-based EWS for honeybee colony collapse. Our results show that the presence of EWS is not equivalent to successful prediction of the transition. The analyzed models exhibit regime shifts accompanied by CSD, but detecting these signals in finite and noisy observations requires longer and more densely sampled time series than typically available for practical monitoring. Moreover, in empirical temperature records, CSD-like trends were detectable but provided limited discrimination between colonies that subsequently collapsed and those that survived. Declining mean temperature provided slightly greater discrimination than conventional CSD indicators, although its predictive value remained modest. Non-Gaussian correlated noise and the imperfect correspondence between hive temperature and colony strength further constrained EWS performance. These findings show that EWS can exist at the dynamical level without becoming useful predictors at the observational level, at least for our case study, thus cautioning against treating CSD-based indicators as generic predictors of ecological collapse.

entry.title: Saddle Buckling of a Multicellular Alga Driven by Differential Growth
entry.summary: During development of many simple multicellular organisms there is a complex interplay between cell growth and generation of an extracellular matrix that confers structure. We study this problem quantitatively using $Gonium~pectorale$, a 16-cell alga that transforms from a flat to a buckled shape during growth without cell division or rearrangement. Cell-level measurements and 3D reconstructions show that the $12$ peripheral cells grow faster than the central $4$, producing hoop stress that selects the saddle mode, whose amplitude displays a continuous bifurcation with classical square root singularity. These results are consistent with a continuum model of differential growth within Föppl--von Kármán theory, which yields information on the mechanical properties of the ECM. Implications of this transformation in evolutionary transitions to multicellularity are discussed.
entry.arxiv:comment: 7 pages, 4 figures plus Supplementary Material and 3 videos (available at website of REG)

entry.title: One-Step Self-Assembling Lipopolymer Coatings Enable Direct Longitudinal Biosensing in Native Biological Matrices
entry.summary: Sample-driven cross-reactivity remains a fundamental bottleneck for sensitive and selective biosensing in complex biological environments, particularly in microfluidic systems where high surface-to-volumes ratios amplify non-specific interactions. Here, we address this challenge with a one-step, biomimetic surface functionalization strategy based on engineered lipid-based nanocarriers that self-assemble within minutes into immunoassay-ready, antifouling interfaces that couple pegylated-lipid passivation with biorthogonal, site-specific probe conjugation. This approach enables rapid, tuneable, and reproducible surface functionalization, which suppresses sample-specific cross-reactivity even in undiluted serum, and supports direct, label-free digital biosensing assays directly in native biological environments. When integrated into an optofluidic platform combining digital in-line holography and microfluidics, this approach allows time-resolved quantification of tetraspanin-positive extracellular vesicle secretion dynamics from two-dimensional and three-dimensional lung cancer cell models using 50 μL of sample within 10 min, without isolation or purification. Because the presented surface functionalization proceeds via self-assembly rather than covalent surface modification, this one-step modular-approach is intrinsically decoupled from device fabrication and applies to both glass and PDMS, coating the entire microfluidic channel, thereby establishing a general route for integrating biomimetic nanostructures into robust, high-performance immunoassays, advancing biosensing beyond end-point measurements, and towards rapid and continuous real-time monitoring.

entry.title: Learning effective stochastic predator and prey dynamics across physical and biological systems from limited data
entry.summary: Constructing an effective low-dimensional stochastic model from sparse observations requires separating deterministic drift from state-dependent fluctuations when the governing interaction law is unknown. We formulate an adaptive neural stochastic differential equation with topology constraints (TC-AdaNSDE) for two-variable predator--prey dynamics. To regularize the inverse problem when data are scarce, the model combines flexible drift and correlated diffusion fields with density-adaptive local Kramers--Moyal moment estimates and soft phase-space constraints reflecting boundary saddle behavior near extinction and local stability near coexistence. Using a known nonlinear stochastic system, we first show that short-time trajectory error cannot assess diffusion accuracy on its own and must be paired with distributional measures of one-step transitions and long-time phase-space occupancy. We then apply this framework to macroscopic turbulence and zonal flow energies reduced from Hasegawa--Wakatani plasma simulations and to short ecological time series. In the sparse-data regime, TC-AdaNSDE reproduces both short-horizon evolution and long-time invariant energy distributions where deterministic reductions collapse and unconstrained stochastic fits diverge, while recovering physically interpretable drift and fluctuation fields across both physical and biological systems.

entry.title: Beyond Final Answers: Interpretable Tumor Immune Microenvironment Reasoning from H&E and mIF
entry.summary: Readouts of the tumor immune microenvironment (TIME), such as CD8+ T-cell density, intra-epithelial infiltration and the Ki67 index, combine tissue architecture from H&E with cell phenotypes from multiplex immunofluorescence (mIF). Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) could automate these readouts with an explanation, but two gaps remain. Pathology MLLMs read H&E alone, while these readouts need the cell phenotypes that mIF measures. And their reasoning has no step-level truth to be checked against, so R1-style reinforcement learning rewards only the final answer and leaves the reasoning unverified. Same-section H&E and mIF provide what both gaps lack: mIF measures every cell without manual annotation, which gives cell-level ground truth for each step that clinical guidelines prescribe, from delineating a tissue compartment to counting and normalizing the marker-positive cells within it. We therefore present HERMES (H&E-mIF Reasoning with Multimodal Evidence Supervision), an R1-style MLLM that reasons jointly over paired H&E and mIF in guideline steps and is trained with a process reward that checks every stated quantity against this truth. Across four field-level TIME tasks in colorectal cancer, HERMES (4B) reaches an average accuracy of 84.5%, compared with 74.7% for the strongest of twelve proprietary, general, medical and pathology MLLMs, and a higher share of its intermediate quantities is correct than for the strongest open-weight baseline. Without the process reward, reinforcement learning barely improves on supervised fine-tuning (80.0% vs. 78.8%) and fewer stated quantities are correct; editing a decisive stated quantity changes the answer as implied in all 885 test questions. Without retraining, it keeps the highest average accuracy on an external cohort imaged with CODEX (76.4% vs. 67.3%) and on head and neck cancer, a cancer type absent from training (76.7% vs. 72.5%).

entry.title: MambaSplit: Severity-Robust and Inference-Efficient Semantic Unmixing of Fluorescence Microscopy Image Data
entry.summary: The number of structures fluorescence microscopy can image in one sample is limited by how few fluorophores can be separated without significant spectral overlap. Semantic unmixing circumvents this limit by imaging two structures in one fluorescent channel and computationally separating the superimposed image into one image per structure. Because pixels rarely identify their structure, unmixing requires both local and long-range spatial context. The relative brightness of the two structures is unknown and can be very uneven, so predictions must remain accurate across mixing severities, from balanced mixtures to ones where a structure is barely visible. Existing methods either process small image patches or add context through auxiliary pathways that slow inference on large images. We present MambaSplit, a hierarchical state-space encoder with a convolutional decoder that captures context across large tiles in linear time and predicts both channels in one deterministic pass. MambaSplit trains either on computationally summed channel images with random mixing ratios, where a lightweight head estimates the unknown ratio and conditions the decoder on it, or on experimentally acquired superpositions. Across five datasets and nine mixing ratios, MambaSplit achieves the highest RI-PSNR, by up to 3.0 dB, in 11 of 15 dataset-severity combinations and ties in one more, while running 5.9x faster than the strongest baseline. On acquired superpositions, fine-tuning a model pretrained on summed inputs matches or exceeds all baselines. Ablations show that accuracy and robustness come mainly from the training recipe: large tiles, mixing ratios sampled across their full range (up to 11 dB over fixed-ratio training), and independently drawn channel crops (3.9 dB on BioSR). The state-space backbone makes large tiles affordable, enabling high-content screening and event-driven smart microscopy.
entry.arxiv:comment: 28 pages, 15 figures, 23 tables; main paper (8 pages) followed by supplementary material

entry.title: The long-term divergence exponent and the temporal structure of step-to-step perturbations: a simulation study in two passive walking models
entry.summary: Purpose. Divergence exponents are used to assess the local dynamic stability of gait. Human experiments have related the long-term exponent ($λ_L$) to the complexity of gait fluctuations. Model studies used perturbations without controlled temporal structure. The question was whether $λ_L$ responds to the temporal structure of perturbations in walkers without neuromuscular control. Methods. Two passive walkers, M1 (pilot) and M2 (exploratory), received step-to-step perturbations of five amplitudes ($σ$) and nine temporal structures (ARFIMA parameter $d$), and human stride series of free and metronome walking. Results. At constant amplitude, $λ_L$ increased with $d$ in both models. It was higher with free series than with metronome series or with surrogates. It did not follow $σ$ in M1 and followed $σ$ in M2. Its double dissociation from the short-term exponent was supported in M1 only. In a descriptive analysis, the condition means of $λ_L$ correlated with the scaling exponent of the step durations ($r = 0.980$ in M1 and 0.906 in M2). Conclusion. In two passive walkers with fixed mechanics, $λ_L$ followed the temporal structure of the perturbations; its specificity depended on the model. This response supports the name attractor complexity index (ACI), proposed for $λ_L$ from human experiments.
entry.arxiv:comment: 49 pages, 6 figures, 2 tables. Includes appendices (2 tables) and supplementary material (1 figure, 8 tables). Code, results and scripts: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24365284

author.name: Philippe Terrier
author.arxiv:affiliation: Haute Ecole Arc Santé, HES-SO University of Applied Sciences and Arts Western Switzerland, Neuchâtel, Switzerland

entry.title: When Foundation Models Disagree: Representational Heterogeneity for Calibrated Uncertainty in Whole-Slide Image Classification
entry.summary: Pathology foundation models supply strong representations for whole-slide image classification, yet the confidence attached to their predictions remains hard to trust. Prevailing uncertainty estimators act within a single feature space and thereby overlook the uncertainty that the choice of foundation-model representation itself induces. This work introduces CALIFUSE, a calibration-oriented framework that fuses several pathology foundation models for the specific purpose of uncertainty estimation. Departing from accuracy-driven fusion, CALIFUSE reads representational heterogeneity across encoders as an explicit confidence cue. Slide-level decision consensus is coupled with chunk-level evidence agreement quantified through Jensen-Shannon divergence, so that both prediction stability and fine-grained evidence consistency inform the estimate. Foundation-model encoders stay frozen. A task-specific nnMIL classifier is still trained for each FM; CALIFUSE then estimates confidence at inference without training an extra fusion module. Evaluated on seven WSI classification tasks under several foundation-model combinations, the framework sharpens calibration, misclassification detection, and selective prediction relative to both the strongest single-encoder baseline and naive ensemble averaging, all while preserving competitive balanced accuracy.

entry.title: Ab-initio cryo-EM reconstruction from moments of denoised images
entry.summary: In single-particle cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM), high-resolution three-dimensional (3-D) refinement requires a reliable ab-initio model to converge to the correct structure. Both refinement and existing ab-initio methods estimate the orientations of the particle images together with the 3-D structure, which can be slow for large and noisy datasets. We present a method of moments approach that bypasses orientation estimation and recovers a 3-D ab-initio model from the first three moments of denoised images. On experimental datasets, our method produces ab-initio models rapidly and successfully initializes high-resolution refinement. This is the first successful application of method-of-moments-based ab-initio modeling to experimental datasets without assuming a uniform distribution of orientations.

entry.title: Prognosis Without Prediction: The Intrinsic Geometry of Survival
entry.summary: Modeling systemic failure in high-dimensional environments is fundamentally limited by supervised algorithms that attempt to predict sparse, noisy or censored endpoints. To break this reliance on explicit outcome regression, we engineered the Self-Organizing Survival Manifolds (SOSM) framework, a deep learning architecture that decouples unsupervised representation learning from survival labels and treats time-to-event progression as an emergent geometric property. The system projects heterogeneous multi-omics arrays into a unified latent space governed by a pseudotime-weighted, curvature-minimizing graph Laplacian, organizing patient trajectories along low-dissipation geodesic flows. To validate the framework, we applied this architecture to a 184-patient clear cell renal cell carcinoma multi-omics cohort. Across a deterministic 5-fold cross-validation pipeline, SOSM achieved a mean Concordance Index of $0.768 \pm 0.068$, while out-of-fold risk stratification yielded significant survival divergence (log-rank $p < 0.001$) accompanied by a 14.7% increase in local manifold dissipation among high-risk patients. Furthermore, interrogating the network's encoder weights confirmed that the model autonomously recovered canonical metabolic and microenvironmental drivers of disease progression without supervised feature selection. By demonstrating that systemic failure can be mapped as a geometric phase transition, SOSM establishes a generalizable computational engine for prognostic modeling across biological, industrial and financial complex systems.

entry.title: Horizontal Flow Matching for Single-Cell Spatiotemporal Dynamics
entry.summary: Learning the spatiotemporal dynamics of cells from spatial transcriptomics requires connecting snapshots of different cells acquired in different coordinate frames. A rotation or translation of a section can appear as cell movement and distort the inferred correspondence. We introduce horizontal flow matching, which learns changes in tissue organization, molecular state, and cell abundance up to shared rigid motion. The dynamics follow a continuity--reaction equation whose action assigns no cost to shared rigid motion, and the resulting horizontal projector removes this component from spatial prediction errors during learning and from predicted velocities during generation. An equivalent endpoint problem jointly estimates correspondence and relative pose in Wasserstein--Fisher--Rao geometry and yields analytic paths whose velocity and growth serve as regression targets. Regressing these targets recovers the horizontal dynamics under ideal population conditions. Our model, HORIZON, uses an equivariant transformer to predict velocity and growth from the current tissue, so that a tissue can be generated continuously from a single initial snapshot. On a simulated tissue observed in perturbed coordinate frames, alignment improves reconstruction and projection reduces rigid drift. On four spatial transcriptomics time courses, HORIZON reconstructs tissue geometry, gene expression, and cell abundance more accurately than existing spatial and unbalanced trajectory methods, and interpolates held-out developmental stages.

entry.title: Elysium: Simulation-Free Unbalanced Schrödinger Bridges
entry.summary: Reconstructing cellular dynamics from snapshots is challenging because the destructive nature of single-cell measurements makes tracking the same cells over time impossible. Cellular dynamics are inherently stochastic and involve changes in population size through proliferation and apoptosis. Growth-based methods represent population change as a rate on the density, which does not assign exits and entries to individual cells. Unbalanced Schrödinger bridges model individual events, but neural solvers for killed diffusion bridges simulate trajectories during training. We introduce Elysium, a simulation-free solver that jointly learns state transition and mass change. Using a killed Brownian reference and its time reversal, Elysium constructs direct regression objectives from an optimal endpoint coupling and conditional bridge distributions, without simulating trajectories during training. We show that the minimizers of the expected training objectives recover the optimal unbalanced Schrödinger bridge. Empirically, Elysium reconstructs state transitions, population size, and event distributions on simulated benchmarks with known killed-diffusion ground truth, outperforming existing deterministic and bridge-based solvers. On single-cell time courses, it interpolates cell state distributions at unobserved time points, tracks population expansion and contraction, and captures biphasic drug-response dynamics.

entry.title: MitoWorld: A Stochastic World Model of the Single-Cell Cycle under Genetic Perturbation
entry.summary: A cell observed after a gene knockdown has an uncertain future, both in how its appearance will evolve and when it will divide. Existing approaches predict endpoints or population-level changes without jointly modeling individual trajectories and division timing. In this work, we present MitoWorld, a stochastic world model that generates these future appearances as continuous evolution in a Gaussian reference latent, terminated by a division hazard and converted into images by a conditional diffusion renderer. The ordinary transition provably preserves its Gaussian reference, tying its noise to its dynamics; paired observations identify its discrete transition where stationary marginals cannot. The hazard turns division timing into a survival likelihood that can be tested against real cycle lengths. On 325 held-out MitoCheck tracks spanning 17 knockdowns and a control, MitoWorld lowers FID by 34.6\% and the video metric JEDi by 45.6\% relative to the strongest baselines. Its latent-space prediction intervals achieve near-nominal 90\% coverage, are 35\% narrower than those of a model with freely fitted noise. The hazard also yields cell-cycle length distributions with KS distance close to the model-based finite-sample reference. Testable single-cell stochastic dynamics thus offer a generative tool for time-lapse perturbation screens.

entry.title: Cardiac MRI-informed electrocardiography enables biologically grounded cardiomyopathy detection
entry.summary: Precise myocardial phenotyping at population scale is limited by the cost and accessibility of cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR), whereas electrocardiography (ECG) is widely available but reflects electrical rather than structural and functional information. Here we develop MyoECG, a cross-modal representation learning framework that distils myocardial structural and functional knowledge from CMR into standard 12-lead ECGs, enabling imaging-informed cardiomyopathy detection and subtype classification from ECGs alone. MyoECG was pretrained on 45,241 paired ECG-CMR examinations from UK Biobank and a tertiary cardiovascular centre, then developed and validated across more than 1.8 million ECGs from seven independent datasets. Across internal and external datasets spanning prevalences of 0.2-54.7%, MyoECG outperformed five pretrained ECG foundation models, with AUROCs of 0.800-0.974 for cardiomyopathy detection. In a multi-reader study of six cardiologists, MyoECG assistance improved mean sensitivity by 0.109 (95% CI, 0.041-0.175; P = 0.009) and specificity by 0.056 (95% CI, 0.004-0.108; P = 0.040). In 41,128 UK Biobank participants, the MyoECG score showed genetic correlations with cardiomyopathy (rg = 0.409) and dilated cardiomyopathy (rg = 0.371), genome-wide associations at four loci, including regions mapped to NFIA and KCNQ1, and associations with 69 circulating proteins related to myocardial stress, cell adhesion, vascular biology and metabolism. The cardiomyopathy correlation attenuated to non-significance after adjustment for 27 measured CMR traits (rg = 0.131; P = 0.143), indicating that the score captures CMR-derived information rather than dataset-specific shortcuts. MyoECG offers a scalable route to CMR-informed cardiomyopathy assessment and a strategy for transferring knowledge from resource-intensive imaging to widely deployable physiological signals.

entry.title: STORM: A Lightweight Structure-Free Model for Binding Affinity Prediction
entry.summary: Accurately predicting a small molecule's binding affinity to a protein, a critical task in drug discovery, remains challenging. Physics-based approaches like free-energy perturbation (FEP) have very high computational costs and require expert setup. Recent machine learning--based cofolding models have reported accuracy approaching that of FEP---and at least one of them, Boltz-2, has already been widely adopted for affinity prediction---but they remain expensive for large computational screens and even more expensive for retraining on newly collected experimental data. To address these challenges, we introduce STORM: Similarity Transfer from Observed Reference Molecules. STORM is a fast, simple machine learning model that ensembles many small model fusions of diverse protein and molecule representations for binding affinity prediction. Trained on the same data, STORM matches or exceeds the accuracy of Boltz-2 on multiple evaluation datasets, while delivering a speed improvement of over five orders of magnitude for both inference and training. Our results also suggest opportunities to substantially improve affinity prediction accuracy by integrating historical experimental affinity data with structural and biophysical information.

entry.title: Structured AI ideation yields physical strategies for epithelial barrier repair
entry.summary: AI systems increasingly support literature analysis, candidate evaluation and hypothesis refinement, but enabling researchers to explore research directions beyond established disciplinary approaches remains challenging. We developed Abelio, an AI system designed to generate novel research directions by expanding investigators' avenues of inquiry. Abelio reformulates research objectives, uses these alternative formulations to identify relevant elements outside conventional disciplinary boundaries, and refines the resulting hypotheses. Each stage integrates divergent exploration with convergent selection through a dedicated subsystem. In quantitative evaluations, proposals generated by the Ideation Core (Abelio's hypothesis-generation core) outperformed those of four frontier large language models in scientific soundness and hypothesis diversity, and three of four in distance from existing literature. Subsystem ablation showed that each subsystem contributes to the property it targets, with the contribution of Element Selection measurable before Refinement. To investigate intestinal epithelial barrier restoration, Abelio proposed physical interventions involving membrane-tethered poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG) and cholesterol-anchored complementary DNA. Both proposals were archived before experimentation and subsequently tested independently in damaged Caco-2 monolayers. PEG preserved barrier function in a membrane-surface-dependent manner, whereas complementary DNA enabled sequence-specific restoration that was reversible on demand. These findings demonstrate how structured research ideation can identify experimentally testable approaches beyond established disciplinary conventions.

entry.title: Fiberpose: state-of-the-art fiber morphometry and instance segmentation with a distance-transform neural network
entry.summary: Analysis of fibrous structures in SEM images is a routine task in biomedical engineering and materials science. However, most available methods for fiber quantification still rely on classical image binarization followed by simple post-processing. These approaches often produce unreliable results in images with weak boundaries, heterogeneous contrast, and densely packed fibers. Here, we introduce Fiberpose, a framework that reformulates fiber analysis as direct regression of a smooth distance-transform (DT) field, together with a novel set of geometry-based algorithms specifically adapted to this representation. The predicted field directly encodes fiber geometry, while the accompanying algorithms enable instance reconstruction and measurement of diameter and orientation within a unified workflow. The framework is implemented as a standalone Python desktop application and a web tool https://fiberpose.org. On an independent dataset of fibrous SEM images, Fiberpose achieved state-of-the-art instance-segmentation accuracy in comparison with SAM2 and Cellpose-SAM, and more accurate diameter measurements than DiameterJ, Fibar and GIFT. The method remains effective in dense and weakly contrasted regions and shows qualitative generalization across microscopy modalities not represented in the training data. Fiberpose therefore provides an interpretable geometric representation and an automated pipeline for reproducible quantitative characterization of fibrous materials.

entry.title: Optimising Recruitment and Sample Allocation in Multi-Site Rare Disease Studies
entry.summary: Clinical research in rare diseases is challenged by the limited availability and broad geographical distribution of eligible patients. This necessitates multi-centre collaboration and strategic selection of analytical laboratories based on capacity, cost, and capability. We present a mathematical framework based on cardinality optimisation to support key operational decisions in study design, balancing clinical relevance, feasibility, budgetary constraints, and logistical factors. The framework was implemented in the Reconstruction and Computational Modelling for Inherited Metabolic Diseases (Recon4IMD) project, aiming to recruit 1,900 diagnosed patients across 24 healthcare centres and eight metabolomic laboratories. Compared to both proportional heuristic and greedy marginal allocation baselines, the proposed optimisation model consistently achieved higher recruitment yields in simulated multi-centre scenarios and reduced metabolomic analysis costs by approximately 30% under unconstrained conditions. Notably, both the heuristic and greedy allocation baselines became infeasible under progressively tighter laboratory capacity constraints, whereas the optimised model maintained feasibility and cost control. These findings highlight the value of integrated optimisation strategies for improving recruitment, platform selection, and sample allocation in complex, resource-limited research settings.

entry.title: Adaptive attention routing multimodal expert graph neural network for drug-drug interaction prediction
entry.summary: Accurate prediction of drug-drug interactions (DDIs) is essential for drug safety in combination therapy. Multimodal methods built on knowledge graphs (KGs) already combine molecular structures, substructures, targets and biomedical relations into drug representations, but they still face three problems: features are heterogeneous across modalities, fusion does not adapt to individual drug pairs, and modality-specific information is diluted during integration. We propose the adaptive attention routing multimodal expert graph neural network (AARME-GNN) to address them. A Feature Adaptive Calibration Module (FACM) reduces within-modality noise in each representation through bottleneck reparameterization and channelwise recalibration before fusion. A Multimodal Weight Router (MMWR) then sets the modality weights of each drug pair, with an entropy constraint that prevents the weights from collapsing onto one modality. A Routing-Aware Weighted Distillation (RAWD) mechanism builds a soft target from the unimodal branches, so that the fusion classifier retains the knowledge held by each modality. On Dataset 1, AARME-GNN improves precision over MKG-FENN by 3.71 and 6.57 percentage points in known drug and known new drug prediction, and the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) by 4.53 in new drug prediction. On Dataset 2, the advantage is concentrated in the two cold-start settings and in precision.

entry.title: OCCAM: Improved Single-Cell Representation Learning and Perturbation Effect Prediction
entry.summary: Predicting the effects of genetic perturbations requires models that generalize beyond observed cell contexts and gene combinations. We introduce Occam, a multilayer perceptron (MLP) framework for representation learning and perturbation-effect prediction. Occam combines cell representations learned through denoising with gene interaction, text, and protein-sequence features. It achieves the highest aggregate representation scores for perturbation information and cell-type preservation with batch integration. In cross-context few-shot prediction, a perturbation and a cell context are each observed during training, but never together. Occam better captures the measured response patterns for these unobserved combinations than four retrained competitors or direct transfer of the same perturbation's measured effects from other training cell lines. Without fine-tuning, Occam best distinguishes perturbations among the evaluated models and simple baselines in cell lines held out from predictor training, across seen and unseen assays. Predicting expression levels accurately in these settings remains challenging. For double perturbations, which target two genes simultaneously, Occam composes learned single-gene responses to better capture the combined response and reduce expression error compared with competing models and summed single-gene effects. These gains extend to both strongly additive and weakly additive responses. Together, these results support simple MLPs for cell representation learning and perturbation-effect prediction across contexts and gene combinations.

entry.title: Calpha: Toward Native Biomolecular Intelligence in a General-Purpose Language Model
entry.summary: Biomolecular foundation models predict the structures of proteins and their complexes accurately, and large language models (LLMs) reason in natural language, but the two remain separate: the abilities of the former are not part of a general-purpose LLM, and the reasoning of the latter does not enter a structure prediction. Calpha aims at one general model that folds proteins and complexes, understands protein sequence and structure, and lets its language reasoning influence the structures it predicts. This report covers the first step, in which an LLM outputs single-chain protein structures. Qwen3.5-9B reads a sequence enriched with ESM2 residue features. It can respond in text or emit a token that invokes a pretrained SimpleFold structure head, which receives information about the protein only through Qwen's residue states. Under a fixed folding request, the head achieves mean TM-scores of 0.808 on the FoldBench-334 development set, 0.635 on CASP16 domains and 0.900 on a CAMEO-style PDB set. We compare these predictions with a baseline in which ESM2-3B encodes the sequence and a fine-tuned SimpleFold-3B head predicts the coordinates. The two systems also differ in trainable weights, training duration and crop length. For chains of 100--299 residues, all three paired confidence intervals include zero. At 300--600 residues, the mean differences are -0.044, -0.160 and -0.025, respectively. In a separate test, four English request types triggered folding on every evaluated example. Protein training reduced accuracy on a 350-item MMLU-Pro subset from 77.4% to 70.3%. An LLM can therefore output single-chain structures from its own states, with lower long-chain scores in the current comparisons and reduced accuracy on the evaluated MMLU-Pro subset. Complex prediction, structure understanding and the effect of language reasoning on the predicted coordinates remain future work.

entry.title: multiCAsp: Spatially Informed Canonical Association Analysis of Multi-Omic Data
entry.summary: Simultaneous profiling of multiple molecular layers at spatially resolved locations creates opportunities to identify shared cross-modal biological variation in its tissue context. We present multiCAsp (multi-omic Canonical Association informed by spatial graph), a probabilistic latent-factor model for integrating $M \geq 2$ spatially resolved omic modalities. It incorporates spatial dependence through a graph-Laplacian prior on shared latent factors and uses an expectation-maximization algorithm to estimate factor scores and modality-specific feature loadings. Because the prior is defined on a neighborhood graph rather than on Euclidean distances, it accommodates irregular tissue geometries and extends naturally to multiple tissue sections. Simulations show that multiCAsp consistently achieves higher mean latent subspace and loading recovery than alternative methods across varying sample sizes, feature dimensions, and noise levels, with the largest gains under high noise. Compared with an existing Gaussian process-based spatial factor model, it is also less sensitive to how the spatial coordinates are represented, produces spatially smoother factors, and has lower computational cost. Applied to metabolomic-proteomic data from macaque cortex and gene-protein data from human renal carcinoma, multiCAsp recovers spatially coherent multi-omic factors with interpretable biological signatures. In the macaque data, transferred factors retain broad spatial patterns across animals and support cross-modal prediction of protein abundances from metabolomic measurements.

entry.title: Weight-Space Programming Changes How an LLM Uses Python for Computational Biology
entry.summary: Weight-space programming allows a language model to edit another model's weights without gradient-based training. We used Claude Opus 5.5 to edit Qwen3.5-0.8B and investigated how the edits changed its use of Python on computational biology problems. We compared four initial edited checkpoints with the original model on 50 test problems across three test seeds, yielding 600 paired evaluations. Strictly correct answers increased from 44 to 77, and technically correct answers, which included correct final values rejected for formatting, increased from 64 to 100. Repeated Python calls decreased from 1,834 to 1,044. Among the 64 pairs in which only the edited response was technically correct, the original model had already computed the correct value in 36 but did not submit a technically correct final answer. The edited model corrected the computation in 13 of the 64 pairs. With six additional checkpoints on the same 50 problems, technically correct answers rose from 96 to 154 across 900 pairs. We explored three selected problems with ten test seeds for each of ten checkpoints. On the melting-temperature problem, correct Python outputs decreased from 60 to 22 while technically correct final answers increased from 0 to 18. Weight editing changed both the calculations Qwen ran and whether it submitted a correct answer.
entry.arxiv:comment: 16 pages, 3 figures, 6 main tables, and 1 supplementary table

entry.title: Beyond AUC: Do Mammography Risk Models Predict When Cancer Occurs?
entry.summary: Longitudinal deep learning models for mammography-based breast cancer risk prediction output either per-year cumulative risks or a discrete distribution over the year of diagnosis, from which cumulative risks F1,...,F5 are derived. These models are evaluated almost exclusively with year-wise AUCs and the concordance index. We show that these metrics are largely insensitive to when cancer occurs: they can be high even for a model that carries no information about the year of diagnosis. We re-evaluate two recent longitudinal models (OA-BreaCR, LMV-Net) on CSAW-CC with a 5-year horizon using timing metrics computed on cancer cases only. Despite C-indices up to 0.75, neither orders cancer cases by time to diagnosis significantly better than chance (c_time 0.51 and 0.55, both 95% CIs covering 0.5). Weighted absolute timing error favours a constant "year 3" prediction over both models, so we use c_time as the primary timing metric. For Mirai's additive-hazard head, also used by LMV-Net, we analyse how per-year increments passed through a ReLU can collapse under severe class imbalance. We also propose a breast-level, two-stage model that separates whether from when. It matches LMV-Net in discrimination (C-index 0.745 vs. 0.746) but orders cancer cases better (c_time 0.58 vs. 0.51, paired 95% CI of the difference 0.01-0.13), on par with Mirai's published weights (0.57).
entry.arxiv:comment: 7 pages, 2 figures, 1 table. Submitted to ISBI 2027

entry.title: Scaling large language model-assisted line-of-therapy adjudication with human-in-the-loop evidence-calibrated selection
entry.summary: Large language models (LLMs) have enabled the ability to scale clinical adjudication tasks traditionally dependent on exhaustive manual review. Line-of-therapy (LoT) adjudication, a major bottleneck in oncology cohort construction, is a prime example. Line boundaries must be inferred from longitudinal treatment histories according to nuanced, study-specific definitions, at every regimen transition for every patient. LLMs can apply this adjudication at scale, but their reliability varies across patients. Treatment histories differ in complexity, and ambiguous or atypical patterns depend on expert clinical judgment. Reliable automation thus requires verified support for model assignments and the ability to identify cases that warrant manual review. Here, we present evidence-calibrated selection (ECS), a human-in-the-loop framework for scaling LLM-assisted LoT adjudication. ECS derives confidence from observed clinician adjudications, prioritizes patients with the least-supported assignments for follow-up review, and returns completed adjudications to the model as precedent. As the evidence base grows, ECS continuously calibrates confidence to estimate residual error, thus enabling more efficient use of clinician time. In simulations on 136 clinician adjudicated patients with multiple myeloma, ECS achieved a residual error of 5% after review of 44.6% of patients, compared to 62.2% when review was directed by LLM self-reported confidence and 81.9% under random sampling. These results support a scalable approach to study-specific LoT adjudication, using clinician evidence to inform automated predictions, minimize error, and reduce review burden.
